Senses.Explanation: Seven hands and eight feet pictures extravagant or disorderly many-limbed action. Zhanran Yuancheng gives the phrase as a direct answer, while Wuzhun, Wuchu, and Duanqiao deploy it in distinct hall talks to expose tangled responses or excessive display. The seven-strip robe enters questions, hall talks, and verse alongside the sound of a bell. Yunmen asks why one puts it on; later speakers use the robe in their own tests and images. In a case Wumen cites, Yunmen Wenyan asks why a monk puts on the seven-strip robe when the world is so broad and the bell sounds. Wumen then warns against following sound and form. The selected robe phrase is Yunmen's old question inside Wumen's case comment. In Yunmen Wenyan's recorded case, the narrator says he removes his seven-strip robe before Yunmen asks a monk whether he might fail to know the teaching in a future life. The monk stays silent and later substitute answers follow. The selected robe word names the garment in the narrated action, not a word Yunmen utters. In a hall sermon Wuyi Yuanlai asks why one wears the seven-strip robe after saying a bell struck his heart and clouds rise from its sound. He gives an image of a canopy descending, then presses listeners to distinguish several positions. The robe phrase links the bell to the monk's clothing in his question. During an evening encounter a monk says bell sound has bitten through the seven strips; Hanyue Fazang takes up the line in his own address about the third day of the twelfth month. He adds frozen pillar and quiet lantern images. The phrase moves from the monk's response into the master's seasonal verse. In a verse on hearing a bell and putting on the robe, Jifei Ruyi says bell sound wears the seven-strip robe and nothing is hidden from the listener. He then comments on Yunmen's bell saying. The phrase recasts the robe as part of the sound scene in his own verse. A monk asks Pinjixiang Zhixiang about presenting the matter face to face. Pinjixiang replies that bell sound bites through the seven-strip robe, then moves to a different question. The phrase is his direct answer using the bell and clothing image.

Senses.PreferredTarget: From seven hundred monks, one is chosen; with nothing there from the start, he draws close.
AlternateTargets: Among seven hundred monks one is chosen; because originally there is nothing, he becomes intimate.
SearchAliases: seven hundred monks one chosen no thing from the start
Senses.Note: Caotang Shanqing's verse describes Huineng receiving the patriarchal robe, and Shipuzhi later uses that verse to challenge an assembly about the robe.

Senses.Explanation: To split, burst, or be exposed completely in every direction. Masters apply the rupture image to frozen constraint, delusion, death barriers, tough practitioners, the sky at awakening, and maneuvering that finally breaks down. Yinyuan contrasts cold splitting in every direction with warm enclosure in many layers. Juelang says recognition inside his circle breaks open the barrier of birth and death. Senses.Explanation: Through on all sides, open in every reach — the corpus's seven-through-eight-reaching binome for the way with nothing blocking it, from the opened Yunmen gate to the old road that runs straight to Chang'an. Yuanwu Keqin, writing to the layman who shared his shrine-niche: it is the one whose root-stock can leave the rafters of expedient roosting who, with a single raising, knows the landing place — and then molts clear through to the seven-eight estate and shows forth great ease; Zhenjing Kewen, ascending the hall: opening the gate of Yunmen, through seven ways and reaching eight — but you must know there is a latch-pin; if you do not know it, alive you are as dead; the yellow dragon's thousand changes must still be followed into the lair where it hides — fail to arrive, and though you have eyes you are blind; worthies, I watch the way of the sovereign of the teaching: the sovereign of the teaching's way is thus — let the one with eyes discern it. Tianyin Yuanxiu, at the small assembly, raises the old case of Nanyuan asking Fengxue how the southern staff is weighed, Fengxue's quaint weighing back, and the staff beneath which no birth-and-death remains — Fengxue's awakening was not nothing, but it fell into the second head; were I Nanyuan, says the master, the moment he opened his mouth to ask how the staff is weighed here, a staff across his spine would guarantee him through seven ways and reaching eight — though today's crude fellows take it as one staff, burying the old sages and blinding not a few eyes; Yinyuan Longqi, holding up the fly-whisk: before the staff-tip has even touched, the whole realm is fully manifest; the nose hangs down, the whole body exposed; take it on entire and you leap past buddhas and patriarchs at a stroke — and if you cannot yet, here I draw one thread of a road for you: shining on heaven and mirroring earth, this shore and that shore through seven ways and reaching eight, and then the great tongs can work, the great function apply — smashing the crowns of buddhas and patriarchs, overturning the patch-robed one's very handle. Sanyi Mingyu, raising the whisk: Wanshou's one old road — through seven ways, reaching eight, straight through to Chang'an; come by boat or come by land, nothing is not possible — only Qianfeng was too spare for you and Yunmen too lavish; I bustle before and behind, lifting and carrying, merely to get you home and able to rest, in the colored robes facing your parents in the front hall, meeting your brothers again under the red-bud tree; Lianyue Daozheng, entering the temple: the gate-court lonely and steep, the inner hall deep — tell me, from where does one enter? — three strikes of the staff: opened through, seven ways and eight, done! And in he goes; Fangrong Ruxi, asked what is the exceeding through the one gate: the seven-through-eight-reaching one does not go — yet you lean on exceeding through a single gate. And the limit, at the hanging of the bell-board: Yinxin Foming Jina lifts the striker — just this use, off this use: the mirror of buddhas and patriarchs, the command of humans and gods — it makes even the seven-through-eight-reaching one, on arrival, hardly escape fumbling hands and flurried feet; grant him three heads and six arms, still he must hear the command and surrender. And what is the proof? He strikes the bell-board: beware hearing it.

Senses.Explanation: Budai, literally 'the Cloth-Bag monk,' is the non-lineage figure defined in Chan records by the bag he carries and uses in public exchanges. His title is attested. Asked 'what is the cloth bag?' (如何是布袋), he puts the bag down; asked 'what is the matter beneath the cloth bag?' (如何是布袋下事), he shoulders it and leaves. Asked the great meaning of the buddha-teaching, he again puts it down and stands with folded hands; asked whether there is an upward matter, he shoulders it and goes. In the street he says he is waiting for a person and rejects the claimant who says he has arrived. Records raise his verse, 'Maitreya, true Maitreya, manifests countless hundreds of millions of bodies, constantly showing himself to people, while people do not recognize him' (彌勒真彌勒，分身千百億，時時示時人，時人自不識), and publicly comment on it. The Zen Budai is thus the bag-bearing street figure whose putting down, shouldering, waiting, displaying, and Maitreya verse are repeatedly raised and judged.

Entries.SourceTerm: 會則事同一家，不會則萬別千差

Senses.PreferredTarget: Understand, and the matters belong to one household; fail to understand, and they differ in countless ways
AlternateTargets: When understood, matters are one family; without understanding, they divide into myriad differences
Senses.Note: The pair says understanding gathers an affair into one household, while lack of understanding leaves countless differences. Qianyan puts it beside an old Linji example; Wuchu applies it to discipline and freedom; Yanxi to heaven and human life; Yungu to scripture and Chan. Each teacher asks listeners to show understanding in a present case. The line turns on their response, not on a simple count of sameness and difference.

The headword is the current introductory voice, not a speech by Dongshan or the elder within that case. It asks what one can actually do with an encounter rather than valuing ornate words as gold. After answering a monk's questions with a raised fist, Kongyin Daodu strikes his staff and explicitly cites red-eyed Guizong's understand-or-circulate pair. Kongyin says he will not follow the ancient teacher's heels: not understanding and conventional circulation can cut off feelings of sage and ordinary. Yet one must penetrate this, or remain a player with mud balls. Striking again, he allows understanding and use along the way to rescue only half. The exact headword is Guizong's quoted formulation; the current teacher reverses and qualifies it, preventing a settled opposition between sacred understanding and worthless worldly activity.

Entries.SourceTerm: 會得箇中意，鐵船水上浮

Senses.PreferredTarget: Understand what this means, and an iron boat will float on water
SearchAliases: understand what this means, and an iron boat will float on water
Senses.Note: An old verse says to protect life by “killing,” to finish the killing before settling for the summer, and then adds: “Understand what this means, and an iron boat will float on water.” The apparent impossibility is its test. Guxue cites the verse at the end of a summer retreat and asks whether the boat names killing or reviving. Yikui asks how one can both protect life and kill it, then ends with the iron boat. Wuzhun recounts a dream in which the verse is preached and turns from the dream to a question about waking. Xiyan voices the verse in another summer talk and invites everyone to board the boat. These teachers use the image to break a flat reading of the old lines.

Entries.SourceTerm: 會醫還少病，知分不多愁

Senses.PreferredTarget: One who knows healing has fewer illnesses; one who knows their measure has fewer worries
AlternateTargets: Knowing medicine means less illness; knowing one’s proper share means less anxiety
SearchAliases: knowing medicine fewer illnesses knowing measure fewer worries

Senses.Note: The first clause says that someone who understands healing has fewer illnesses. The second turns from medicine to knowing one’s own measure or portion, and so having fewer worries. Foyan pairs the lines in a verse about meeting and sharing wine; Shitian, Shuzhong, and Liaotang reuse the pair to settle separate addresses. The saying works as a concise check on needless striving, not as medical advice or a promise that a healer never falls ill.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 平云：汝心便是。洞山云：雖然如是，猶是某甲疑處。興平云：恁麼即問取木人去。大眾，者些子見不破、踏不著，饒伊辯如滿慈、智如鶖子，未免癡狂外邊走。今夜正當群陰剝盡、一陽來復之時，聊與諸人聚話片時，敢問諸人：且洞山與麼問、興平與麼答，莫是將錯就錯、借路經過麼？莫是真實相為、拳踢相赴麼？如斯品論，鄭州出曹門。只如興平末後云：恁麼即問取木人去。此一轉語太殺慈悲，多少人向者裏錯會？有能於此撥開胸襟、伸得口氣，何止醍醐灌頂？苟或未然，陋巷不騎金色馬，回來却著破襴衫。上堂。若以語言名狀心，終不得心；不以語言名狀心，亦不得心。去此二途，如何湊泊？驢唇先生開口笑，阿脩羅王打𨁝跳，海神失却夜明珠，擘破毗盧穿七竅。成道，上堂。一明一切明，一了一切了，豁開總持門，諸法不相到。六年冷坐，舌上生茅；夜覩明星，眼中添翳。以手拍禪牀左邊，云：釋迦老子過者邊著。就中若有識機宜、別休咎底，必然別有生涯。下座。上堂，舉：僧問古德：如何是冬來事？德云：京師出大黃。拈云：會醫還少病，知分不多愁。除夜，小參。靈山會上，少室巖前，的的相傳，將錯就錯。德山小參不答話，鈎頭有餌；趙州小參要答話，秤尾無星。七十三，八十四，築著磕著，礙塞殺人。看看今夜是年窮，箇箇明朝添一歲。靈不在己，聖不慕他，檢點將來，不是不是。洪祐和尚送歸源法衣至，上堂。拈衣示眾云：者箇是先歸源，向異類中遺下皮可漏子，日炙風吹而不壞、刀斫鋸解而不開，業力既重，累及不肖子亦入其羣隊去也。披云：且道是驢？是馬？遂陞座，乃云：夫為宗師者，垂一機、示一境，如青天霹靂不容掩耳、如十日並照無幽不燭、如大爐鞴煆煉頑鈍、如大醫王療種種病、如大舟航運載一切，有如是奇特、如是作略，然後方可據法空座傳持大法，為人抽釘拔楔、解粘去縛，明頭合、暗頭合，據虎頭、收虎尾。若也向上論去，尚恐埋沒宗風，恥他先作，那更婆婆和和、淟淟涊涊，撒土拋沙，瞎學者眼，豈堪稱譽？天台那畔、石佛山前，有大智人把斷要津，不通水泄，提破沙盆，索起遼天重價，用黑豆法換盡大地人眼睛，掀翻舊日條章、裂破今時窠臼，直得德山、臨濟吞聲飲氣，竺乾、震旦逈絕行踪，灼然不落聖凡，實謂大功不宰。諸人還知落處麼？經天緯地無多子，扶樹單傳只一人。復舉：阿難問迦葉：世尊傳金襴外，別傳何法？迦葉召阿難，阿難應諾。迦葉云：倒却門前剎竿

Senses.Explanation: The phrase “Somewhat closer” is a comparative verdict: one response is judged nearer than another without being declared complete. Somewhat closer or a little better by comparison. The phrase is attested and repeatedly serves as a qualified public appraisal. Huangbo Xiyun says that among Mazu Daoyi’s eighty-four teachers only Guizong Zhichang is somewhat closer. Xitang Zhizang summons the assembly and says that the record's unnamed participant who tries to help is somewhat closer. After an interlocutor whom the record does not name says he does not understand, Guanghui Qingshun replies that this is a little closer. Baiyan Fu says that Fu Dashi, Baozhi, and Emperor Wu still do not compare quite as well with Yan's action. Yuanwu Keqin says that being entirely unlike a list of proposed identifications is only then somewhat closer, and immediately asks why. Changqing Huileng applies the phrase after a long silence. The comparison can therefore qualify speech, silence, action, withdrawal, or the condition before a question while still withholding full approval.
